utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented by Novak Lukic and Mr. Guy-Smith as Defence counsel. We have Ester Brilliant with us today for the first time in the courtroom and Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Just to place on the record that the Chamber is still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge David is still indisposed. Before we start the business of the day, I would like just to talk about the order of the Trial Chamber on the 65 ter summaries issued on the 28th of May and the responses that came from the parties with respect to that. Let me just say, it is all very well for parties to take points, but it doesn't advance the trial of this case if we are going to take semantic technical points which don't take us anywhere. When the Defence case began, the Defence was supposed to have given the entire 65 ter list and summaries to the Prosecution to enable the Prosecution to prepare to cross-examine the witnesses. The Defence was not ready to do so. In the spirit of accommodating the Defence, the Chamber ordered that the Defence will give 15 names at a time two weeks in advance until such time as you are able to give the entire list. To now come and argue that you didn't say the 16 witnesses you are going to call are the next witnesses is to play with time and to waste the Court's time. And irrespective of what your submission might have said that it did not have the word next, the court order said that the 15 that you call or the 16 that you call shall be the next because what is the purpose of giving us the 15 if they are not the next, if you are going to call them at the end of the trial. They can only be the next people that you are going to call as your witnesses in the case until such time as you have given the entire 65 ter list. So let us stop playing. Let us get on with the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if my understanding of what you said is correct, but the gist of it is as follows: The list of 15 witnesses that we submitted is a list of witnesses that we intend to call in that order. However, we also have the intention of calling other witnesses in respect of whose summaries objections were not made, and they would fit in somewhere in between. So if we have a witness for whom the Prosecution is already ready or for whom the Trial Chamber deems the summaries fine, we don't see why we could not fit him in even though we have the list of 15 witnesses. We have met all the requirements of the guide-lines. We have listed all the witnesses that are to be called until the summer recess, so we've gone even beyond what is necessary in order to ensure that the Prosecution may be able to prepare themselves. In addition to the 15 witnesses that we listed, there is also a witness we intend to call whose summary is not objectionable. Now, our problem is of course to fit this witness in order to call him only at the end of these 15 witnesses, and we don't feel that this is in the spirit of the Trial Chamber's guide-line, that this is indeed what the Prosecution needs to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if that's what you intend to do, that's what you should have said in your submission. You didn't say so in your submission. Let me remind you also that on the 1st of June as the last point of discussion, the Chamber asked the Defence whether they had any comments to make on that order of the Court and Mr. Lukic said, we will comply. We've seen the order and we will comply. Now, instead of complying, you gave a list of only seven witnesses instead of the 15, Mr. Lukic. For starters, which is the point I didn't raise now. And then you queried the use of the word "next," and what I'm talking about is the use of the word "next." I'm saying, irrespective of what submissions you might have made that you don't intend them to be the next, the Chamber orders you to call them next. If you have others, obviously that you have given before and that the Prosecution is ready to cross-examine, that's a matter between you and the Prosecution. And if you want to say, you want to fit them in, say so, which you didn't say in your submission. You are now making the submission for the first time today. And I don't want to belabour this point, all I'm just saying is let's get on with the work. I hope you have now delivered the entire 15 to the Prosecution and that by the date stated in a previous order, you'll submit the balance of the 65 ter list witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give me a moment, please, to consult with my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I might. It is our intention to get the work done. It is not our intention to dawdle. It is our intention to have available to the Prosecution that information that they need for purposes of preparing their cross-examinations. I, as you know, I was not in court at the last session and that may or may not have caused some of the difficulty and to the extent that it has, I do apologise, and take it upon my shoulders with regard to the issue of "next." And with regard to the issue of "next," we can a lengthy or short conversation. I'm going to leave it alone. Obviously there was some miscommunication to extent that miscommunication existed. I did not consider that we were making a new submission, to the extent that it seems that we are. Once again, that was not my intent and I apologise. It is my present understanding the following exists: The Prosecution is in possession of all, but I think, and I'm just asked to verify this, I think all but seven 65 ter summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All but seven or are they in possession of seven?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, all but seven. I think it's all but seven that are in dispute. Or to which they felt they did not have sufficient information. That is what I believe is the present state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is the but seven the part of the 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, when you say all but seven I need to understand: Are you talking about the entire 65 ter list --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- of the Defence? In other words, you've complied with the first part of the order, you've given them the 15 that they were supposed to get. Now, with the remaining balance of your entire witnesses you've given them all but seven or is it all but seven as part of the 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this is where I think -- this where I think that we continue to have a level of confusion that I am going to attempt to remedy in two ways. There are seven remaining 65 ter summaries irrespective of how you wish to identify them for which the Prosecution has sought further information out of the entirety of the Defence list. Out of those seven, two of them will be submitted by the close of business today. That leaves us with five 65 ter summaries out of the entire list of the Defence for which there is some open issue. With regard to that five, that particular group of five, that particular group of five is part of the five that has been included in the discussion for some period of time, and I'm saying this in a general term because I don't want to misstate the record in any fashion whatsoever. What we did do in our last submission was we submitted to the Chamber and to the Prosecution those witnesses who would be called between now and the the summer recess. Those would be the next seven witnesses. Thereafter at the present time as we stand here today or as I stand here right now, there is no further indication of who the first witness would be after the summer recess. Okay. So to the extent there is -- there is discordance between the Chamber's order of the next 15 and the situation that we are in right now, it would be fair to say that at the present time we have not said who the witnesses will be when we begin again after the summer recess. We have supplied to the Prosecution 65 ter summaries at this point in time that will include, and that's from the entirety of all the Defence witnesses, that will include the next witnesses that we call after the summer recess. I hope -- I hope -- I hope that that clarifies the situation in which we are in and what we were trying to do is do this in an orderly fashion because, among other things, and this is recognising with the number 15 does exist, and also once again asserting and both strongly and gently we have no desire to play any games, that once we come to the summer recess, among other things, we are going to be engaged in further re-assessment of how we are going to present the Defence after the recess begins. So there will be, we believe, necessarily, a re-adjustment not only of order of witnesses but number of witnesses. So we were trying to do it in the most orderly fashion that we could. If we have caused problems or we have caused confusion, once again I apologise, that was not my intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Your apology is accepted. You will appreciate that you are dealing with issues that the Chamber has not raised. The Chamber has not raised anything about what is going to happen after the recess, and therefore the Chamber is going to confine itself to the issues that was raised by the Chamber. Accepting as I do what you have told the Chamber, that you have provided all 65 ter summaries to the Prosecution but seven, and to the extent that the submissions by the parties relating to the issues raised by the Chamber this morning require an order of the Court, this is the order of the Court: The Defence is ordered to comply with the order of the 28th of May 2010 fully. I say this because Chamber is not going to give a written order or a written decision, that is the order, and I say this notwithstanding what you say that you have complied. If you have complied then there's nothing for you to do. If you haven't complied, the Chamber orders you to comply timeously. Mr. Harmon, I don't know whether you do want to say anything. I know the Chamber has now given an order, but you may wanted to have been heard maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm satisfied with the Court's order, I will wait to see what compliance with it follows. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That done, then are we ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I interrupt, you Mr. Guy-Smith. There is just one other point that I've just been reminded of which we needed to raise. The next point we'd like to raise is the fact that in the last sitting, the last two sittings we sat pursuant to 15 bis. We still pursuant to 15 bis today. On the last two occasions, no evidence was led, and if the parties agree that those two sittings could be seen as, what, 65 ter meetings or housekeeping meetings, we can then sit 15 bis for the entire week. However, if the parties don't agree then we'll only sit for three days. What I'm told is that you would need a little more time for your next witness and you would like to finish that witness and let him go. The Chamber does not want to rule on this. It wants to hear the parties' position on this. Starting with you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Prosecution agrees, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm being Mr. Lukic just for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based on the Chamber's analysis, that is the last two sittings were housekeeping sittings and we are defining them as such, the Defence agrees because the Defence would like to be able to use the entirety of this week for purposes of obtaining testimony. We are going to do it for this limited purpose at this particular time and don't want to be in a position where at any point in the future is this interpreted as we are acceding to anything, other than with regard to the specific situation given some of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A precedent is not being created, it is based specifically on the facts of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, we agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let the parties agree on that, that being the case, then your next witness, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we call the next witness, if we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may now be seated and good afternoon to you. Madam usher, we are in open session, if you might lift the blind for us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please state your full name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Skrbic, lieutenant-general, and I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Skrbic, during your testimony, I believe we will be cautioned a number of times, me probably more than you, by the interpreters to make pause between questions and answers. I would kindly ask you to try and bear that in mind and you can follow the text on the screen in front of you which may serve as an indication when to start answering. Can you tell us how old you are and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of October, 1946, so I'm 63, 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Apologies, I was born in the village of Hotkovci, Glamoc municipality, which is now part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It used to be Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I wanted to go briefly through your career and perhaps you can confirm the details I will specify. I will also dwell on certain parts of your career because I believe it is relevant for these proceedings. In any case, you completed the military academy in 1968; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your specialty is that of rocket artillery, or perhaps you can tell us more precisely what your specialty is in military terms?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The general specialty is anti-aircraft defence and my immediate specialty is rocket units without the artillery part you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your military career you went through all the levels from a rank-and-file soldier to a commanding officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I went through all the stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also specialised in another thing which is your degree in military political matters at the higher political school of the JNA in Belgrade. You also have a degree in military sociology and psychology; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The high military political school is something I completed in 1977. Following that, I began teaching in that school. I taught dialectics of society which is in the field of philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then between 1985 and onwards, first you were a desk officer and then you reached a level of chief of department in what used to be called the political administration of the secretariat for national defence in Belgrade, and later on it became an administration for political education; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were quite precise in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see parts of Mr. Skrbic's personal file, which is P1688. However, this part was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That can't be part of P1688 if it's not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. The B/C/S version was admitted but the Prosecutor skipped this part. I know, I know, that is why I will ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what is admitted, the English version, what is the controlling language for admission? English or the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we may spend a lot of time discussing this issue because there is an issue with admission, although I believe it should be settled out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only reason I'm asking is that, you know, if the Registrar pulls up P1688 and you are quoting something that is not part of it, then we are not going to find it. I'm not trying to waste time here I'm just being practical. So if it is outside P1688 then we either call it by whatever ERN number it is and you can ask later to be added to P1688 or you can ask a new number for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just notified by my Case Manager that this page is part of P1688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Then it is P1688.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN number is 0611-5210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll have Mr. Registrar determine what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in B/C/S and 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record the English translation is 0611-5209. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we can keep the English version on the screen. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the bottom part, Mr. Skrbic. This is what's relevant for these proceedings. It says here, I'm reading the one-but-last box from the bottom. It says that in the federal Secretariat for the National Defence, you were with the morale administration as of the 27th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 29th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic, can you just say again which box are you reading and what do you mean by box here? There are columns and what have you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the B/C/S version does not correspond to the English page we have. It seems that this break in the proceedings took its toll, we are now being assisted by the Registrar. I thank him for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have just seen this entry, Mr. Skrbic, did you perform these duties within the period as specified?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It is correct. Perhaps I can be of assistance. The fourth column contains the date you mentioned, the 29th of July, 1991. I was appointed then as chief of morale guidance section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next column --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the -- that's the third column, not the fourth column, am I right? I see 29th July, 1991, in my third column and my fourth column shows me above that 28th of July, 1991, which deals with independent officer for NIR in humanities. But chief of morale guidance section in the first department is 29th of July, 1991, in the third column, am I right? I'm looking at the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the penultimate column, Your Honour, in the English translation and in the B/C/S it says, witness, that you were sent to another military district in Sarajevo by a decision of the federal secretariat of the 25th of April, 1992. Were you indeed sent to the 2nd Military District as per that decision at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As is specified here, I was ordered by the personnel administration of the federal Secretariat for National Defence that I was supposed to be sent to the 2nd Military District; however, I did not go for completely different reasons. However, I was ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss that later. After the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia came into existence on the 10th of July, 1992, as specified here in the administration for moral guidance and education in sector for PVM, perhaps you can assist me with what that means?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Legal affairs and moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, you were appointed to that position on the 10th of July, 1992, following which, until the 11th of November of the same year you were appointed chief of department for internal information in the same administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This administration, was it attached to the General Staff or the Ministry of Defence at the point when the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ was established?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The administration was attached to the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I saw the abbreviation MO here, and I wanted us to be quite precise on this score. Thereafter as stated in your personnel file on the 17th of December, 1993, pursuant to an order of the chief of the personnel administration of the General Staff of the VJ, you were temporarily assigned to the personnel centre at the Belgrade garrison, this is the 30th personnel centre, and then on the 12th of February, 1994, pursuant to the same commanding officer's order, you were assigned to the position of the assistant commander for moral guidance at the 30th Personnel Centre of the General Staff of the VJ. Let me ask you this: Where were you, in fact, assigned to and where did you, in fact, go on the dates specified in this file?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of December, 1993, I went to the 2nd Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska de facto. There I was assigned the duty of the assistant commander for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of the 2nd Krajina Corp. That was the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever assistant commander for morale in any -- or moral guidance in any of the units of the corps of the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page in the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are three entries in manuscript, we will get back to them later. Here we have three similar entries starting with the 13th of January, 1997, according to which you were designated to be a stand-in. We have the same entries but the dates are different. At the 13th, or rather, at the 30th Personnel Centre, and you were supposed to be assistant chief of the personnel administration within that centre, it's just the dates that differ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will go back to this particular status you held, but this period between the 13th of January, 1997, and the 31st of December, 1999, did there exist a decision on your appointment to a duty within the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I did not have a decision appointing me to a duty within the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought I was alone in this problem so I wasn't going to complain, but it looks like everybody or some people are having problems with LiveNote. Shall we take an early break and let the technicians look at the problem, please. Court adjourned. Come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the documents again on our screens, the ones that we looked at earlier. Oh, excellent, they are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go through them and complete the topic of your professional career. Can we have -- or rather, what I'm reading is the bottom part of the English translation. Pursuant to a decision of the 31st of December, 1999, you were appointed to the position of a deputy of the information and moral guidance administration of the General Staff of the VJ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last position you held before your retirement, again pursuant to a decision of the president of the FRY, was your position as chief of the administration up until your retirement, again pursuant to a decision of the president of the FRY, as of the date of the 31st of December, 1999. You were discharged from your duties in the VJ on the 31st -- on the 3rd -- on the 31st of March, 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you somewhat. It was not pursuant to a decision that I became the chief of the same administration, rather, I became the chief of the information administration with the Federal Ministry of Defence. In other words, I was transferred from the VJ General Staff to the Federal Ministry of Defence. The rest is correct, as you've described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My apologies. You completed your professional career in the Ministry of Defence of the FRY. I have a couple of questions left, but we will be going back to this topic during your testimony. It has to do with your ranks. I will be going through the ranks that we find relevant for this trial only. In your personnel file, it is stated that you were given the rank of major-general on the 27th of December, 1995, and that's with the VJ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you were promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general, which is the rank you held upon your retirement on the 14th of September, 1999, again in the Army of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the degrees you hold and the positions you held, can you tell me if you hold any other diplomas from any high-level educational institutions of the JNA and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Upon graduation from the military, I attended the military political school of the JNA, and this is something that I've mentioned earlier. Previously, I also graduated from the rocket and anti-aircraft defence school, this was also post-military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that in addition to these military schools, you've also got your masters degree from the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade in 1983, so you hold a master in political science and the topic was freedom as a value and raison d'etre of society; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Javier, are you okay? You're okay. Thank you, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question which may be relevant for this trial. Mr. Skrbic, you have already appeared as a witnesses before the ICTY, according to the information I have, you testified in the Popovic et al. case as a Prosecution witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was a Prosecution witness in that case and I testified, therefore, before this Tribunal previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to certain facts that I should like us to focus during your testimony. I will be going through your professional career and as I do, we will be covering certain topics. The first of these topics is your work with the administration for moral guidance and information, first with the SSNO and then with the VJ General Staff. And let's start with 1991. Since before us we have a gentleman who is versed in these matters, can you tell us what was the standing of morale in the JNA in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In view of the analyses I worked on at the time which largely had to do with the morale in the people's -- Yugoslav People's Army, we had a number of indicators which we obtained based on scientific research, based on interviews with army personnel, troops, officers, and civilians employed in the JNA. It was elements dictated by the situation which determined the morale in the JNA. Primarily, it had to do with the disintegration of Yugoslavia in all the various seams, the start of the armed conflicts in the territory of the SFRY, the cessationist elements in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. All these elements made themselves felt in the aspect of morale which was steadily falling and this was also due to the fact that the role of the JNA became increasingly uncertain. The entire personnel, be it ordinary soldiers or officers, felt that there were no prospects in that institution. Then there was the inflow of refugees from Slovenia, Croatia, among whom there were also JNA servicemen. These were individuals who were homeless, in a way, who found themselves in a very vulnerable position materially speaking, and who came to the territory of the FRY as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there and perhaps I should be more specific in my question. Since you were part of the administration for morale and information, what sort of treatment was the JNA accorded by the mass media across the FRY? I'm referring to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: These letters seem to be appearing very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to look at the screen. Suffice it that you wait for a few seconds before answering my question.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: After awhile, I joined a specially formed group within the SSNO which engaged in analysing the way in which the JNA was viewed and analysed by the mass media across Yugoslavia. Based on our work, we concluded that the JNA came under increasing attacks by the media which took it upon themselves to turn the population, especially in Slovenia, against the JNA, especially so in Croatia, and the tendency spilled over to Bosnia-Herzegovina and lastly to Serbia. Montenegro and Macedonia were not that prominent in that sense. The media attacks encouraged physical attacks on the JNA. They first manifested themselves in power cuts, in the cuts in water and food supplies to the JNA barracks, and these eventually escalated into physical attacks on the barracks in Slovenia, Croatia, and then Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. To cut the long story short, let me say that we produced a study which we prepared for the Federal Executive Council of the SFRY, which was in actual fact the government. The study or the analysis we made was forwarded to this institution, and it was supposed to alert them to the possible remedies that needed to be found in such a situation. I don't know what became of this analysis, to tell you the truth. It did contain information highlighting the problems, the role, and the position of the JNA at the time. This is something that I haven't really presented in great detail now and perhaps there's no need for that at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position taken by your administration, and did you formulate this position of yours to your superior structures with regard to the JNA presence in Slovenia and, of course, I'm referring to the events that transpired there in 1990 and 1991 and the armed conflict that ensued there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I remember quite clearly the conversation that several of us had with the chief of the moral guidance administration of the SSNO on what it was that we were supposed to give as a proposal with regard to the JNA status in Slovenia. Our unanimous conclusion was that we should suggest that the Yugoslav People's Army peacefully withdraw from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position taken by your administration with regard to the JNA and the fact whether it should stay in Croatia? Was this -- and Bosnia-Herzegovina, was this something that you formulated as a proposal for your superiors?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The position on the status of the JNA in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was somewhat different. This because we suggested that the JNA should remain in the territory of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina where it was supposed to play a delicate role, that of preventing any ethnic conflicts, of protecting the JNA barracks, and of facilitating peaceful withdrawal of the JNA troops from Slovenia on their way through Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And let me just add one thing. We were aware of the fact that the role we wanted to give the JNA was a very complex one. Still what we bore in mind were the constitutional and legal provisions regulating the role and status of the JNA which, in a nutshell, stipulated that the JNA should preserve and maintain the constitutional order, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning this topic and the description of the level of morale of the JNA in that period, I'm now referring to 1991 and 1992 this time round, what was the response to the call-up both of the reserve and the officers' ranks in the JNA, particularly if you could distinguish if there was any between JNA and VJ starting from 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: With respect to your question, I would like to state that the strength of the JNA in the period that you discuss started being weakened substantially. Slovenia, Croatia, and partly Bosnia-Herzegovina invited troops and officers of the JNA to leave the JNA and guaranteed that the fact of their desertion, although that was -- that would be treated as desertion under the laws in force, that they would not feel any legal consequences of such an act. And for that reason it was necessary to mobilise some parts of the reserve contingent to fill up the numbers. At the time mobilisation in Croatia and to an extent in Bosnia was pointless. We simply did not even attempt to mobilise people in those areas. Let me finish. In Serbia and Montenegro, initially mobilisation was partly successful only to start dwindling away given that particularly in the territory of Serbia different groups started coming up and started launching protests against mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are going to try our first attempt with the new documents. Could we please see on the screen the document 1D12-0090. And the draft English translation would be [in English] ET 1D12-0330. 0325. [Interpretation] That will be the English version. B/C/S page will have to be rotated, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But while we are trying to do that, let me read out several excerpts from this document and by reading out slowly, I hope to aid our interpreters in the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: English reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: English, 1D12-0325. [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's first take a look at this page, Your Honours. Mr. Skrbic, during proofing for your testimony, I had an opportunity to show you some of these excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to the next page in the B/C/S. Well, the same page but the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I showed you these documents and but the right-hand side. I showed you these documents and elicited your comments during proofing the way that I'm going to ask you during your testimony. I'm going to go through some of the parts and would like you to testify about the facts contained therein. What we see here on the screen is briefing of the commander organs to corps commander. The date is the 15th of July, 1991. It is known to everybody in this courtroom that at the time Mr. Ratko Mladic was chief of staff of the 9th Corps of the military and navy district, the headquarters was in Knin. Did you know where he was in 1991 in July since you had many contact with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When I came to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and after the war in particular, when General Mladic recounted his career, I found out that he was Chief of Staff of the 9th Corps and the commander of that corps, as far as I can remember, was General Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. First of all, two things I would like to raise with you. We don't tell the witness an answer and then ask him the question. You ask him the question and he answers the question. Okay. Secondly, when the witness answers you've got to -- I've been seeing this happening quite a bit this afternoon, you know, try to listen to what the witness is saying and focus the witness on your question. Why I say we don't tell a witness the answer and then ask him the question, you'll see at page 34, lines -- starting from line 14, you say: "What we see here on the screen is briefing of the commander organs to the corps commanders, the date is that. It is known to everyone in this courtroom that at the time Mr. Ratko Mladic was the chief of the staff of the 9th Corps of the military and navy district, the headquarters was in Knin. Did you know where he was in 1991?" You've just told him. There is the problem. And then the answer he gives has nothing whatsoever to do with the question. He's telling us of when he came into the staff of Republika Srpska and after the war in particular, no longer in 1991. After the war, General Mladic recounted his career and I found out that he was chief of the staff of the 9th Corps and the commander of that corps as far as I can remember. It doesn't answer to the period 1991, so listen to the question and make sure that the witness answers your question because the whole discussion becomes meaningless even to the Chamber. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of this diary entry, since this is the first diary entry that is sought to be utilized in this case, I think the first procedural issue is a request to add this to the 65 ter list. I haven't seen a motion to that effect. I think that's the first step. If there's an English translation, I will say we don't have an objection. Generally -- second of all, if there is an -- only in B/C/S, then with would ask that it be MFI'd, but from a procedural point of view, and I don't want to be hyper-technical, but I think it's been the procedure in our case thus far that new exhibits have to be added to a 65 ter exhibit list first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that Mr. Harmon. You know, documents are just called and put on the screen without us knowing where they come from, whether they come from the Mladic diaries or where they come from. And, yes, if we had known we would have intervened. However, it is also your responsibility to intervene at the beginning, not in the middle of the use of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I agree. I was waiting for Mr. Lukic to do that and I waited, I should have intervened earlier. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I should have done the procedural bit and I understand what Mr. Harmon is saying. In the morning I discussed this process situation with Mr. Saxon, and I informed them that the Defence has an intention of amending the 65 ter list whereby we would maybe adduce some parts if not all package 410. When we amend our 65 ter list, first we wait for to receive the translations into English before we consolidate that, and as I said to Mr. Saxon today, Defence intends to MFI this document. And at the moment when we amend our 65 ter list and the Prosecution gives a green light, and if you approve, then we would move to give an exhibit number to this document or those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may very well be, Mr. Lukic, but do remember that the Chamber is not privy to your discussions with Mr. Saxon this morning, so when you come into court, for purposes of procedure, you say I've discussed this with my colleague, he has no objections, however, I make a formal request that this be added to the 65 ter and may I use it in evidence today. And the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Absolutely. I meant to say it at the very end of analysing this document. I should have done it at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure where we are on this. I think I had asked that it be -- the procedural matter be done now. Mr. Lukic wants to do it later. I think for clarity's sake that it be done now at each excerpt that's available. I don't want to wait until either at the end or at the -- some other day in the future where there are -- his testimony about his excerpt, and then it may or may not appear on a later list. I think for purposes of management, I think it's easier that -- well, we don't have a motion yet, to take each excerpt and make an oral motion for a 65 -- an oral application for a change in the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that is the correct procedural way to do it. And I know that right through this trial a mistake has happened where documents went in and then they were MFI'd to be decided later. That's really not the correct procedure. The correct procedure is admissibility must be ruled on before we use the document and then the document can be tendered into evidence. Mr. Lukic, I would suggest that late as it might be in the day, this may just be an appropriate time then for you to make your oral application.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully endorse this. I was led by a decision during a Prosecution case where first we MFI documents and then tender them, but this is more useful, I think, so that I propose orally that this document amends the 65 ter list. This document from page ERN 0668-3833 to 0668-3838 in the B/C/S version as uploaded in e-court. And if necessary, should I give this document a 65 ter number, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, let's clarify some of this. Documents that have been MFI'd so far were MFI'd because there was a debate about the admissibility at the beginning, and the parties agreed we'll mark them for identification and we'll look at their admissibility later. We don't just use documents without asking for that admission and then say, okay, we are following the motions. Secondly, for purpose -- I'm not quite sure whether these are the only pages that you are going to tender at this part of the diary, or are you going to expand on them later during your questioning of this witness, and if you are, maybe the 65 ter number can be given when you have expanded all of them. But if this is all you are going to use with this witness, maybe, yes, you might perhaps give a 65 ter number, depending on how Mr. Registrar thinks that will affect his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the situation is this document is not yet on your official 65 ter list. Fine. First of all, you asked to add it to your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Second, give it a 65 ter number, and finally you are going to ask that it be admitted. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Prosecution's position that the document be added to the 65 ter list of the Defence and that it be used -- it is tendered into evidence and be given a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I was trying to clarify, Your Honour, is whether the range, the ERN range given by Mr. Lukic, 3833 to 3838 included English translations for all of those pages, because if it does not, and I can only see one page on the screen, if it does not, then I would ask that it be MFI'd. So I just seek clarification from Mr. Lukic as to whether that ERN range includes English translations completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is a draft translation that we uploaded, I propose that this be MFI'd until we've received an official translation. This portion has not been received by -- by us from the CLSS as an official translation. And the English translation reflects those B/C/S pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Lukic, that the English translation that we see here is not the official CLSS translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then the official position is that there is no English translation and therefore this must be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed. And to that extent you have no objection, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
